claim: The TEA domain (TEAD) transcription factor forms a transcription co-activation complex with the key downstream effector of the Hippo pathway, YAP/TAZ.
source: The TEA domain (TEAD) transcription factor forms a transcription co-activation complex with the key downstream effector of the Hippo pathway, YAP/TAZ.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the TEAD-YAP/TAZ complex.

claim: TEAD-YAP controls the expression of Hippo-responsive genes involved in cell proliferation, development, and tumorigenesis.
source: TEAD-YAP controls the expression of Hippo-responsive genes involved in cell proliferation, development, and tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about TEAD-YAP function.

claim: Hyperactivation of TEAD-YAP activities is observed in many human cancers and is associated with cancer cell proliferation, survival, and immune evasion.
source: Hyperactivation of TEAD-YAP activities is observed in many human cancers and is associated with cancer cell proliferation, survival, and immune evasion.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by literature.

claim: Mammalian TEAD transcription factors (TEAD1–4) possess auto-palmitoylation activities.
source: We previously reported that the mammalian TEAD transcription factors (TEAD1–4) possess auto-palmitoylation activities and contain an evolutionarily conserved palmitate-binding pocket (PBP), which allows small-molecule modulation.
evidence: This is a previously reported finding by the authors.

claim: Mammalian TEAD transcription factors contain an evolutionarily conserved palmitate-binding pocket (PBP).
source: We previously reported that the mammalian TEAD transcription factors (TEAD1–4) possess auto-palmitoylation activities and contain an evolutionarily conserved palmitate-binding pocket (PBP), which allows small-molecule modulation.
evidence: This is a previously reported finding by the authors.

claim: TM2 shows potent inhibition of TEAD auto-palmitoylation both in vitro and in cells.
source: Representative analog TM2 shows potent inhibition of TEAD auto-palmitoylation both in vitro and in cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TM2 adopts an unexpected binding mode by occupying not only the hydrophobic PBP, but also a new side binding pocket formed by hydrophilic residues.
source: Surprisingly, the co-crystal structure of the human TEAD2 YAP-binding domain (YBD) in complex with TM2 reveals that TM2 adopts an unexpected binding mode by occupying not only the hydrophobic PBP, but also a new side binding pocket formed by hydrophilic residues.
evidence: This is supported by the co-crystal structure data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TM2 potently and specifically suppresses TEAD-YAP transcriptional activities.
source: RNA-seq analysis shows that TM2 potently and specifically suppresses TEAD-YAP transcriptional activities.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TM2 exhibits strong antiproliferation effects as a single agent or in combination with a MEK inhibitor in YAP-dependent cancer cells.
source: Consistently, TM2 exhibits strong antiproliferation effects as a single agent or in combination with a MEK inhibitor in YAP-dependent cancer cells.
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation assay data presented in the manuscript.

claim: YAP and TAZ are the major downstream effectors of the evolutionarily conserved Hippo pathway that controls organ size and tissue homeostasis.
source: Yes-associated protein (YAP) and transcriptional coactivator with PDZ-binding motif (TAZ) are the major downstream effectors of the evolutionarily conserved Hippo pathway that controls organ size and tissue homeostasis (Pan, 2007; Yu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: YAP/TAZ hyperactivation is frequently linked to tumorigenesis in a broad range of human cancers.
source: Beyond their critical roles in development, accumulating evidence shows that YAP/TAZ hyperactivation is frequently linked to tumorigenesis in a broad range of human cancers (Harvey et al., 2013; Pan, 2010; Zanconato et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: YAP/TAZ alone cannot interact with DNA.
source: Importantly, YAP/TAZ alone cannot interact with DNA; therefore, it requires the binding of transcriptional factors TEA/TEF-domain (TEAD1–4 in mammals and Scalloped in Drosophila) to regulate the expression of Hippo-responsive genes (Wu et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: YAP/TAZ requires the binding of transcriptional factors TEAD1–4 to regulate the expression of Hippo-responsive genes.
source: Importantly, YAP/TAZ alone cannot interact with DNA; therefore, it requires the binding of transcriptional factors TEA/TEF-domain (TEAD1–4 in mammals and Scalloped in Drosophila) to regulate the expression of Hippo-responsive genes (Wu et al., 2008; Zhao et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The transcriptional targets of the TEAD-YAP/TAZ complex are involved in cell proliferation, cell survival, immune evasion, and stemness.
source: The transcriptional targets of the TEAD-YAP/TAZ complex are involved in cell proliferation, cell survival, immune evasion, and stemness (Moroishi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Direct targeting YAP/TAZ with small molecules has been shown to be difficult.
source: However, direct targeting YAP/TAZ with small molecules has been shown to be difficult.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Pharmacological disruption of TEAD-YAP/TAZ has been considered as a promising avenue for cancer therapy.
source: Therefore, pharmacological disruption of TEAD-YAP/TAZ has been considered as a promising avenue for cancer therapy (Holden and Cunningham, 2018; Johnson and Halder, 2014; Pobbati and Hong, 2020; Zanconato et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A peptide termed 'Super-TDU' was designed to block the TEAD-YAP interaction.
source: For instance, a peptide termed 'Super-TDU' was designed to block the TEAD-YAP interaction (Jiao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: 'Super-TDU' has been shown to suppress gastric cancer growth.
source: 'Super-TDU' mimics TDU domain of VGLL4, which competes with YAP/TAZ for TEAD binding, and has been shown to suppress gastric cancer growth.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Peptide-based inhibitors generally suffer from poor cell permeability and pharmacokinetic properties.
source: However, peptide-based inhibitors generally suffer from poor cell permeability and pharmacokinetic properties, limiting their therapeutic applications.
evidence: This is established knowledge in drug development.

claim: TEAD-YAP binding interface is shallow and spanning a large surface area.
source: Since TEAD-YAP binding interface is shallow and spanning a large surface area, it is particularly challenging to optimize small molecules for desired potency.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge.

claim: TEAD auto-palmitoylation plays an important role in regulation of TEAD stability and TEAD-YAP binding.
source: Previously, we and others discovered that TEAD auto-palmitoylation plays an important role in regulation of TEAD stability and TEAD-YAP binding, and loss of TEAD palmitoylation leads to inhibition of TEAD-YAP transcriptional activities (Chan et al., 2016; Holden et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Loss of TEAD palmitoylation leads to inhibition of TEAD-YAP transcriptional activities.
source: Previously, we and others discovered that TEAD auto-palmitoylation plays an important role in regulation of TEAD stability and TEAD-YAP binding, and loss of TEAD palmitoylation leads to inhibition of TEAD-YAP transcriptional activities (Chan et al., 2016; Holden et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The lipid chain of palmitate inserts into a highly conserved deep hydrophobic pocket.
source: More importantly, structural and biochemical studies illustrated that the lipid chain of palmitate inserts into a highly conserved deep hydrophobic pocket (Chan et al., 2016; Noland et al., 2016), away from TEAD-YAP interface, which is suitable for small-molecule binding and suggests that lipid binding allosterically regulates TEAD-YAP activities.
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: The palmitate-binding pocket is away from TEAD-YAP interface and is suitable for small-molecule binding.
source: More importantly, structural and biochemical studies illustrated that the lipid chain of palmitate inserts into a highly conserved deep hydrophobic pocket (Chan et al., 2016; Noland et al., 2016), away from TEAD-YAP interface, which is suitable for small-molecule binding and suggests that lipid binding allosterically regulates TEAD-YAP activities.
evidence: This is supported by citations and inference from structural data.

claim: Lipid binding allosterically regulates TEAD-YAP activities.
source: More importantly, structural and biochemical studies illustrated that the lipid chain of palmitate inserts into a highly conserved deep hydrophobic pocket (Chan et al., 2016; Noland et al., 2016), away from TEAD-YAP interface, which is suitable for small-molecule binding and suggests that lipid binding allosterically regulates TEAD-YAP activities.
evidence: This is an inference from structural and biochemical studies.

claim: Flufenamic acid (FA) has been shown to bind to the lipid-binding pocket of TEAD.
source: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug, flufenamic acid (FA), has been shown to bind to the lipid-binding pocket of TEAD (Pobbati et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: FA lacks potency to block TEAD function.
source: Although FA lacks potency to block TEAD function, it demonstrates that the lipid-binding pocket could indeed accommodate small-molecule binding.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: FA scaffold has been extensively explored by medicinal chemists to design TEAD inhibitors.
source: Ever since then, FA scaffold has been extensively explored by medicinal chemists to design TEAD inhibitors, including irreversible inhibitors TED-347 (Bum-Erdene et al., 2019), DC-TEADin02 (Lu et al., 2019), MYF-01-037 (Kurppa et al., 2020), K975 (Kaneda et al., 2020), as well as reversible inhibitor VT103 (Tang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: K975 and VT103 showed strong antiproliferation effects in vitro and antitumor effects in vivo.
source: Among the reported inhibitors, K975 and VT103 showed strong antiproliferation effects in vitro and antitumor effects in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: K975 and VT103 only have effects in limited cell lines, such as NF2-deficient mesothelioma cells.
source: However, these inhibitors only have effects in limited cell lines, such as NF2-deficient mesothelioma cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Most of the reported TEAD inhibitors are irreversible inhibitors targeting the cysteine at the palmitoylation site.
source: In addition, most of the reported TEAD inhibitors are irreversible inhibitors targeting the cysteine at the palmitoylation site, which might have undesired nonspecific reactivity toward other cysteines or other targets.
evidence: This is established knowledge about existing TEAD inhibitors.

claim: MGH-CP1 inhibited transcriptional output of TEAD-YAP in vitro and in vivo.
source: We previously developed a non-FA-based reversible TEAD inhibitor, MGH-CP1 (Li et al., 2020), which inhibited transcriptional output of TEAD-YAP in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: MGH-CP1 only showed sub-micromolar potency against TEAD palmitoylation in vitro.
source: However, MGH-CP1 only showed sub-micromolar potency against TEAD palmitoylation in vitro and was used at low micromolar range in cellular assays.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: TM2 exhibits strong inhibition of TEAD2 auto-palmitoylation in vitro with an IC50 value of 156 nM.
source: Among them, TM2 exhibits strong inhibition of TEAD2 and TEAD4 auto-palmitoylation in vitro with the IC50 values of 156 nM and 38 nM, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TM2 exhibits strong inhibition of TEAD4 auto-palmitoylation in vitro with an IC50 value of 38 nM.
source: Among them, TM2 exhibits strong inhibition of TEAD2 and TEAD4 auto-palmitoylation in vitro with the IC50 values of 156 nM and 38 nM, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Palmitoylation of both exogenous Myc-TEAD1 and endogenous Pan-TEADs is significantly diminished by TM2 in HEK293A cells.
source: In addition, palmitoylation of both exogenous Myc-TEAD1 and endogenous Pan-TEADs is also significantly diminished by TM2 in HEK293A cells, which further confirms its potency and mode of action in cellular context.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The co-crystal structure of TEAD2 YBD in complex with TM2 uncovered a novel binding mode of the compound, which extended into a previously unknown hydrophilic side pocket adjacent to the PBP.
source: The co-crystal structure of TEAD2 YBD in complex with TM2 uncovered a novel binding mode of the compound, which extended into a previously unknown hydrophilic side pocket adjacent to the PBP, and caused extensive side-chain rearrangements of the interacting residues.
evidence: This is supported by the co-crystal structure data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TM2 binding caused extensive side-chain rearrangements of the interacting residues.
source: The co-crystal structure of TEAD2 YBD in complex with TM2 uncovered a novel binding mode of the compound, which extended into a previously unknown hydrophilic side pocket adjacent to the PBP, and caused extensive side-chain rearrangements of the interacting residues.
evidence: This is supported by the co-crystal structure data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TM2 significantly inhibits YAP-dependent liver organoid growth ex vivo.
source: Further functional studies showed that TM2 significantly inhibits YAP-dependent liver organoid growth ex vivo and inhibits proliferation of YAP-dependent cancer cells as a single agent or in combination with a MEK inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TM2 inhibits proliferation of YAP-dependent cancer cells as a single agent or in combination with a MEK inhibitor.
source: Further functional studies showed that TM2 significantly inhibits YAP-dependent liver organoid growth ex vivo and inhibits proliferation of YAP-dependent cancer cells as a single agent or in combination with a MEK inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A library containing about 30,000 non-proprietary medicinal chemistry compounds was screened using click-ELISA assay.
source: To identify new chemotypes that could inhibit TEAD auto-palmitoylation, we screened a library containing about 30,000 non-proprietary medicinal chemistry compounds with three rounds of click-ELISA assay (Lanyon-Hogg et al., 2015) through the Astellas-MGH research collaboration by using the recombinant TEAD2 and TEAD4 YBD proteins.
evidence: This describes the screening methodology used in the study.

claim: Several hits share a common 4-(3-(2-cyclohexylethoxy)benzoyl)-piperazine-1-carboxamide moiety.
source: We found several hits that share a common 4-(3-(2-cyclohexylethoxy)benzoyl)-piperazine-1-carboxamide moiety (data not shown, with micromolar potency in TEAD palmitoylation assays in vitro).
evidence: This is supported by screening data from the study.

claim: Phenyl substituent showed stronger inhibition on TEAD2 auto-palmitoylation compared to heteroaryl group.
source: Compared to heteroaryl group, phenyl substituent showed stronger inhibition on TEAD2 auto-palmitoylation (TM2 vs. TM22, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Hydrophilic groups at the left cyclohexyl ring significantly decrease the activities of TEAD inhibitors.
source: As illustrated by TM45 and TM98, hydrophilic groups at the left cyclohexyl ring significantly decrease the activities, while the phenyl moiety at the right side of the urea moiety is well tolerated (TM112, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The phenyl moiety at the right side of the urea moiety is well tolerated in TEAD inhibitors.
source: As illustrated by TM45 and TM98, hydrophilic groups at the left cyclohexyl ring significantly decrease the activities, while the phenyl moiety at the right side of the urea moiety is well tolerated (TM112, Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: TM2 dramatically suppresses Myc-TEAD1 palmitoylation in cells in a dose-dependent manner.
source: As Figure 1E shows, TM2 dramatically suppresses Myc-TEAD1 palmitoylation in cells in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Treatment of TM2 significantly inhibits endogenous TEAD1–4 palmitoylation.
source: Furthermore, treatment of TM2 also significantly inhibits endogenous TEAD1–4 palmitoylation using an antibody recognizing pan-TEADs (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: At 100 nM, Pan-TEAD palmitoylation was diminished by TM2.
source: Even at as low as 100 nM, Pan-TEAD palmitoylation was diminished.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TM2 is a potent and pan-inhibitor of palmitoylation of TEAD family proteins.
source: Collectively, these results suggested that TM2 is a potent and pan-inhibitor of palmitoylation of TEAD family proteins.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data presented.

claim: TM2 is more potent than K975, VT103, and MGH-CP1 in TEAD2 auto-palmitoylation assay.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, TM2 is more potent than the other three TEAD inhibitors in TEAD2 auto-palmitoylation assay.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: TM2 showed stronger activities in blocking endogenous pan-TEAD palmitoylation compared to K975, VT103, and MGH-CP1.
source: In addition, TM2 showed stronger activities in blocking endogenous pan-TEAD palmitoylation compared to other compounds (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: VT103 is a TEAD1-specific inhibitor.
source: VT103 showed stronger activities on TEAD1 palmitoylation, consistent with the previous report that VT103 is a TEAD1-specific inhibitor (Tang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: TM2 is a more potent and broader pan-inhibitor of TEADs than K975, VT103, and MGH-CP1.
source: Taken together, these data suggested that TM2 is a more potent and broader pan-inhibitor of TEADs than K975, VT103, and MGH-CP1.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data presented.

claim: The co-crystal structure of TEAD2 YBD in complex with TM2 was determined at 2.4 Å resolution.
source: To gain insights into the precise binding mode of TM2, we determined the co-crystal structure of TEAD2 YBD in complex with TM2 at 2.4 Å resolution (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the structural data presented.

claim: TM2 binds to the same PBP in TEAD2 where palmitic acid and other inhibitors target.
source: Overall, TM2 binds to the same PBP in TEAD2 where palmitic acid (PLM) and other inhibitors target (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the co-crystal structure data.

claim: The (2-cyclohexylethoxy)phenyl moiety of TM2 is surrounded by several hydrophobic residues, including F233, L383, L390, F406, I408, Y426, and F428.
source: As shown in Figure 2B, the (2-cyclohexylethoxy)phenyl moiety of TM2 is surrounded by several hydrophobic residues, such as F233, L383, L390, F406, I408, Y426, and F428, enabling strong hydrophobic interactions, which is very similar to the interaction mode of TEAD with the fatty acyl chain of palmitic acid.
evidence: This is supported by the co-crystal structure data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The urea moiety of TM2 exhibits a completely different orientation from palmitic acid and sticks into a new side pocket.
source: Unlike palmitic acid with its head group pointing toward residue C380, the urea moiety of TM2 exhibits a completely different orientation and sticks into a new side pocket, which has never been reported before to be involved in TEAD inhibitor binding and is only accessible by rearranging the side chains upon TM2 binding (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the co-crystal structure data.

claim: The new side pocket has never been reported before to be involved in TEAD inhibitor binding.
source: Unlike palmitic acid with its head group pointing toward residue C380, the urea moiety of TM2 exhibits a completely different orientation and sticks into a new side pocket, which has never been reported before to be involved in TEAD inhibitor binding and is only accessible by rearranging the side chains upon TM2 binding (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the co-crystal structure data and comparison with previous structures.

claim: TM2 binding drives significant conformational changes in the side chains of residues C343 and L374.
source: TM2 binding drives significant conformational changes in the side chains of residues C343 and L374, which makes space for TM2 insertion (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the co-crystal structure data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: TM2 binding causes the side-chain movement in residues Q410 and Y333, which reduces the distance between the nitrogen atom of Q410 and the oxygen atom of Y333 from 4.9 Å to 2.7 Å.
source: Additionally, TM2 binding causes the side-chain movement in residues Q410 and Y333, which reduces the distance between the nitrogen atom of Q410 and the oxygen atom of Y333 from 4.9 Å to 2.7 Å to allow the formation of favorite electrostatic interaction (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the co-crystal structure data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: All eight interacting residues in the new side pocket of TEAD2 are highly conserved among all the TEAD family members.
source: It showed that all eight interacting residues in the new side pocket of TEAD2 were highly conserved among all the TEAD family members.
evidence: This is supported by structural alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The key residues within the newly identified binding site are conserved, even in TEADs from other species.
source: Besides, the protein sequence alignment also demonstrated that the key residues within the newly identified binding site were conserved, even in TEADs from other species (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: MGH-CP1, VT105, and K975 adopt almost the same binding mode as PLM and fit very well with the PBP.
source: Consistent with previously reported results, MGH-CP1, VT105, or K975 adopts almost the same binding mode as PLM and fits very well with the PBP.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: TM2 dramatically blocked the association of YAP with endogenous TEAD1 as well as pan-TEAD in a dose-dependent manner.
source: YAP co-immunoprecipitation (IP) experiments indicated that TM2 dramatically blocked the association of YAP with endogenous TEAD1 as well as pan-TEAD in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by co-IP experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: After treatment of TM2, the expression levels of CTGF and ANKDR1 were significantly suppressed at both 24 and 48 hr.
source: After treatment of TM2, the expression levels of CTGF and ANKDR1 were significantly suppressed at both 24 and 48 hr, while Cyr61 showed strong response at 48 hr (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cyr61 showed strong response to TM2 treatment at 48 hr.
source: After treatment of TM2, the expression levels of CTGF and ANKDR1 were significantly suppressed at both 24 and 48 hr, while Cyr61 showed strong response at 48 hr (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: TM2 treatment substantially altered the gene sets at PC1 in NCI-H226 cells.
source: The samples were plotted and indicated that TM2 treatment substantially altered the gene sets at PC1 in NCI-H226 cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by PCA data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: YAP signature was among the top 3 enriched signatures according to the Normalized Enrichment Score (NES) in GSEA analysis.
source: It showed that YAP signature was among the top 3 enriched signatures according to the Normalized Enrichment Score (NES) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: YAP/TAZ signature was significantly enriched in downregulation phenotype in both Cordernonsi_YAP_conserved_Signature and YAP_TAZ-TEAD Direct Target Genes.
source: Consistently, YAP/TAZ signature was significantly enriched in downregulation phenotype in both gene sets (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: TM2 showed comparable effects with K975 on target genes regulation.
source: TM2 showed comparable effects with K975 on target genes regulation, visualized by heatmap analysis (Figure 3G), and both compounds showed stronger modulation of YAP-target genes than VT103.
evidence: This is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: TM2 and K975 showed stronger modulation of YAP-target genes than VT103.
source: TM2 showed comparable effects with K975 on target genes regulation, visualized by heatmap analysis (Figure 3G), and both compounds showed stronger modulation of YAP-target genes than VT103.
evidence: This is supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The NES for TM2, K975, and VT103 treatment are −2.64, −2.56, and −2.31, respectively.
source: Furthermore, we carried out GSEA of TEAD-YAP/TAZ target genes with TM2, K975, and VT103 treatment, and the NES are −2.64,–2.56, and –2.31, respectively, for the three compounds (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), suggesting that TM2 likely showed better TEAD-YAP/TAZ target genes enrichment.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: TM2 likely showed better TEAD-YAP/TAZ target genes enrichment compared to K975 and VT103.
source: Furthermore, we carried out GSEA of TEAD-YAP/TAZ target genes with TM2, K975, and VT103 treatment, and the NES are −2.64,–2.56, and –2.31, respectively, for the three compounds (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), suggesting that TM2 likely showed better TEAD-YAP/TAZ target genes enrichment.
evidence: This is an inference from the GSEA data.

claim: YAP activity has been shown to be critical for the growth of liver organoid.
source: YAP activity has been shown to be critical for the growth of liver organoid (Planas-Paz et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: TM2 impaired the sustainability of organoids' growth in a dose-dependent manner, with more than 85% of disruption at 40 nM.
source: As shown in Figure 4A, TM2 impaired the sustainability of organoids' growth in a dose-dependent manner, with more than 85% of disruption at 40 nM.
evidence: This is supported by organoid viability data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Ki67-positive cells for organoids maintenance in 3D culture were significantly diminished upon TM2 treatment.
source: Consistently, Ki67-positive cells for organoids maintenance in 3D culture were significantly diminished upon TM2 treatment (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Organoid size was significantly reduced with TM2 treatment.
source: Our results showed that organoid size was significantly reduced with TM2 treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), indicating that TM2 inhibited organoids' growth.
evidence: This is supported by organoid size measurement data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: YAP activation leads to overgrowth of liver organoids.
source: These data are consistent with previous observation that YAP activation leads to overgrowth of liver organoids (Yimlamai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Activation of Hippo signaling is required to maintain differentiation states of hepatocyte.
source: Recent evidence demonstrated that activation of Hippo signaling is required to maintain differentiation states of hepatocyte (Lee et al., 2016; Yimlamai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: TM2 significantly induced the expressions of Alb and Fxr in organoids.
source: TM2 only showed minor effects on cyp3a expression, but significantly induced the expressions of Alb and Fxr (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that TM2 might induce hepatic differentiation of the organoid.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: TM2 might induce hepatic differentiation of the organoid.
source: TM2 only showed minor effects on cyp3a expression, but significantly induced the expressions of Alb and Fxr (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that TM2 might induce hepatic differentiation of the organoid.
evidence: This is an inference from the gene expression data.

claim: NF2 and LATS2 are frequently observed to be inactivated in malignant mesothelioma.
source: NF2 and LATS2, the upstream components of Hippo pathway, are frequently observed to be inactivated in malignant mesothelioma (MM), leading YAP activation in more than 70% of analyzed primary MM tissues (Murakami et al., 2011; Sekido, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: YAP activation occurs in more than 70% of analyzed primary MM tissues.
source: NF2 and LATS2, the upstream components of Hippo pathway, are frequently observed to be inactivated in malignant mesothelioma (MM), leading YAP activation in more than 70% of analyzed primary MM tissues (Murakami et al., 2011; Sekido, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: NCI-H226 cells exhibited striking vulnerability to TM2 treatment with an IC50 value of 26 nM.
source: As shown in Figure 4C, NCI-H226 cells exhibited striking vulnerability to TM2 treatment with an IC50 value of 26 nM, consistent with its potency in blocking TEAD palmitoylation in vitro and in cells.
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: TM2 significantly inhibits cell proliferation of MSTO-211H cells with an IC50 value of 94 nM.
source: Consistently, TM2 also significantly inhibits cell proliferation of MSTO-211H and NCI-H2052 cells (Figure 4D) with IC50 values of 94 nM and 157 nM, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: TM2 significantly inhibits cell proliferation of NCI-H2052 cells with an IC50 value of 157 nM.
source: Consistently, TM2 also significantly inhibits cell proliferation of MSTO-211H and NCI-H2052 cells (Figure 4D) with IC50 values of 94 nM and 157 nM, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: TM2 shows no significant inhibition in the Hippo WT mesothelioma cells, NCI-H28 with IC50 >5 µM.
source: In comparison, TM2 shows no significant inhibition in the Hippo WT mesothelioma cells, NCI-H28 with IC50 >5 µM (Tanaka et al., 2015; Figure 4D), suggesting that TM2 is specific to YAP-activated cancer cells.
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: TM2 is specific to YAP-activated cancer cells.
source: In comparison, TM2 shows no significant inhibition in the Hippo WT mesothelioma cells, NCI-H28 with IC50 >5 µM (Tanaka et al., 2015; Figure 4D), suggesting that TM2 is specific to YAP-activated cancer cells.
evidence: This is an inference from the cell proliferation data.

claim: TM2 and K975 displayed comparable inhibitory effects on cell proliferation in YAP-dependent mesothelioma cells.
source: Overall, TM2 and K975 displayed comparable inhibitory effects on cell proliferation in YAP-dependent mesothelioma cells.
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: TM2 did not exhibit strong inhibition on cell proliferation of HCT116 and DLD1 colorectal cancer cell lines.
source: However, TM2 did not exhibit strong inhibition on cell proliferation of two CRC cell lines (Figure 4D), HCT116 and DLD1.
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Suppression of Hippo transcriptional activities in CRC alone might not be sufficient to inhibit cell growth.
source: These results suggested that suppression of Hippo transcriptional activities in CRC alone might not be sufficient to inhibit cell growth, as observed in mesothelioma.
evidence: This is an inference from the cell proliferation data.

claim: YAP is capable of rescuing cell viability in HCT116 with loss of function of KRAS.
source: Indeed, YAP are found to be capable of rescuing cell viability in HCT116 with loss of function of KRAS, implying that KRAS signaling might also account for lack of potency of TM2 in CRC.
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Strong inhibitory effects and substantial synergy were observed when combining TM2 with MEK inhibitor trametinib in HCT116 and DLD1 cells.
source: Encouragingly, we observed strong inhibitory effects and substantial synergy in both of the two cell lines (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 4), suggesting that combining TEAD inhibitors with other therapies might be a good strategy to broaden their therapeutic applications in near future.
evidence: This is supported by drug combination data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: Combining TEAD inhibitors with other therapies might be a good strategy to broaden their therapeutic applications.
source: Encouragingly, we observed strong inhibitory effects and substantial synergy in both of the two cell lines (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 4), suggesting that combining TEAD inhibitors with other therapies might be a good strategy to broaden their therapeutic applications in near future.
evidence: This is an inference and speculation from the drug combination data.

claim: The much more hydrophobic part of TM2 features a cyclohexyl ring that exquisitely fits the palmitoylation pocket.
source: It showed that the much more hydrophobic part of TM2 featured a cyclohexyl ring, exquisitely fitting the palmitoylation pocket, which is the most well-known structure feature for targeting TEAD (Dey et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the co-crystal structure data.

claim: The side pocket occupied by TM2 is not occupied by all other known TEAD inhibitors, such as MGH-CP1, VT105, and K975.
source: This binding site is not occupied by all other known TEAD inhibitors, such as MGH-CP1, VT105, and K975.
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison data.

claim: The side pocket is not fully available in the palmitate-bound TEAD2 structure, but is formed with significant side-chain rearrangement upon TM2 binding.
source: This side pocket is not fully available in the palmitate-bound TEAD2 structure, but is formed with significant side-chain rearrangement upon TM2 binding.
evidence: This is supported by the co-crystal structure data.

claim: The side pocket is endowed with higher hydrophilicity than the lipid-binding pocket.
source: Moreover, this side pocket is endowed with higher hydrophilicity than the lipid-binding pocket, providing potentials for enhancing drug-like properties.
evidence: This is supported by the co-crystal structure data and analysis.

claim: The novel binding model expands structural diversity of the TEAD-binding pocket.
source: The novel binding model expands structural diversity of the TEAD-binding pocket and will boost the discovery of more novel chemotypes, contributing to the development of therapeutics targeting TEAD-YAP.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural data.

claim: Therapeutic effects of TEAD inhibitors are mainly limited to mesothelioma models.
source: In human MPM, a type of tumor that is highly associated with YAP activation, TM2 showed striking antiproliferation efficacy as a single agent, which is consistent with the fact that therapeutic effects of TEAD inhibitors are mainly limited to mesothelioma models (Kaneda et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: YAP has been shown to converge with KRAS and can rescue cell viability induced by KRAS suppression.
source: Indeed, YAP has been shown to converge with KRAS and can rescue cell viability induced by KRAS suppression (Shao et al., 2014), suggesting that inhibiting YAP activities might be also rescued by other oncogenes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Inhibiting YAP activities might be rescued by other oncogenes.
source: Indeed, YAP has been shown to converge with KRAS and can rescue cell viability induced by KRAS suppression (Shao et al., 2014), suggesting that inhibiting YAP activities might be also rescued by other oncogenes.
evidence: This is an inference from previous work.

claim: Significant synergy effects were observed when combining TM2 with a MEK inhibitor.
source: Consistently, significant synergy effects were observed when combining TM2 with a MEK inhibitor.
evidence: This is supported by drug combination data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Rationalized combination of TEAD inhibitors with other inhibitors could significantly expand the utilities.
source: These encouraging results suggested that rationalized combination of TEAD inhibitors with other inhibitors could significantly expand the utilities.
